messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 65
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 46

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tane Haumia is a 65-year-old widowed Māori man working as a project manager for a mid-sized construction firm in Auckland-born but now based in Honolulu, where he relocated following his wife's death several years ago. He presented to an outpatient psychology clinic reporting significant distress, sleep disruption, and what he described as an inability to "get out from under" an experience that had occurred nearly three years prior. His PCL-5 score of 46 placed him firmly in the clinical range, and across the first two sessions a coherent and painful picture emerged.

The precipitating event was his youngest daughter Aroha's sudden collapse at home from a severe asthma attack when she was nine years old. Tane had been the only adult present. He recalled watching her lips turn blue as she struggled to draw breath, her small chest heaving with a desperate, laboured rhythm he could not stop. He had called 911 and attempted to follow the dispatcher's instructions, but by the time paramedics arrived she had lost consciousness. She survived, but spent four days in the paediatric intensive care unit before stabilising. For Tane, those four days — and especially the twenty minutes alone with her before help arrived — became the fixed point around which his entire inner world reorganised.

In the weeks following Aroha's discharge, Tane found himself returning obsessively to what he had done and, more precisely, what he believed he had failed to do. He had come to believe, with a certainty that resisted all counter-evidence, that his slowness in recognising the severity of her symptoms had caused the crisis to escalate. He told himself he should have known — should have acted faster, kept better medications in the house, been more vigilant. The conviction that he had failed to protect his daughter calcified into a broader self-doubt: he could no longer trust his own judgment in any situation that carried stakes. This cluster of self-blame and perceived failure did not remain contained to his private thoughts. It began to colour how he perceived the world around him, making ordinary situations feel saturated with the potential for catastrophe. When a work deliverable ran behind schedule or a subcontractor didn't return a call promptly, Tane found himself certain that something had gone wrong — that delay meant disaster, in the same way that his own delay had nearly cost Aroha her life. His body kept pace with his mind: his heart would race, his chest would tighten, and on the worst occasions he would notice his own breathing becoming shallow and laboured — a sensation that pulled him instantly back to the living room floor, to Aroha's face.

It was these physical echoes that proved most destabilising. Any encounter with breathlessness, his own or another's, acted as a direct portal to the original scene. At work, when a colleague returned from a run and stood panting in the corridor, Tane had to excuse himself. He began avoiding the annual occupational health checks his employer required, finding reasons to reschedule, then simply not booking them at all. He stopped visiting Aroha's paediatrician with her, delegating that role to her older sister. Hospitals, ambulances glimpsed on the highway, even the antiseptic smell of a pharmacy — all of it he routed around. To manage the intrusive imagery that broke through regardless, he kept his mind in constant motion: long hours at the construction site, podcasts running through the night, volunteer work on weekends. He told himself this was coping. What it was, in practice, was a way of never sitting still long enough to examine the belief that he was a man who could not be trusted to keep the people he loved safe. Because he never examined that belief, it never softened. And because it never softened, every reminder of the event — every breathless colleague, every delayed email, every routine medical form — arrived carrying its full freight of threat.

What finally brought Tane to seek help was a mandatory pre-employment medical required for a new project contract. He sat in the waiting room, heard a child coughing in the next bay, and walked out before his name was called. Standing in the car park, he realised he had not seen a doctor himself in nearly three years. What he feared most, he said quietly in session, was that he would never stop waiting for the next thing to go wrong. What he hoped for, with considerably less certainty, was that he might one day be able to trust himself again.
